questions.subject: AP Biology
questions.question:
Isolated mitochondria are suspended in oxygenated buffer containing succinate, ADP, and inorganic phosphate. Investigators continuously measure O2 consumption and ATP production. At baseline, both are high and steady. At time 1, oligomycin (a specific inhibitor of ATP synthase) is added: ATP production stops and O2 consumption falls to about 15% of baseline. At time 2, with oligomycin still present, 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP, a lipid-soluble molecule that carries H+ across the inner membrane) is added: O2 consumption rises to roughly 130% of baseline, while ATP production remains at zero.

Which statement best accounts for the rate of O2 consumption observed after DNP is added?

choices.A: DNP collapses the H+ gradient, relieving the electrochemical backpressure that had slowed proton pumping, so electron transport to O2 accelerates; no ATP forms because the gradient is dissipated and ATP synthase is still inhibited.
choices.B: DNP accepts electrons from succinate and delivers them directly to O2, bypassing the cytochromes, so O2 consumption rises while no protons are pumped and no ATP can be made.
choices.C: DNP displaces oligomycin from ATP synthase and restores its activity; ATP is synthesized rapidly but is immediately hydrolyzed by the enzyme running in reverse, so no net ATP accumulates.
choices.D: Because ATP synthase is inhibited, unused ADP accumulates and allosterically stimulates the electron transport complexes, raising O2 consumption while ATP output stays at zero.

questions.explanation: Electron transport is thermodynamically coupled to the proton-motive force it generates. When oligomycin blocks ATP synthase, protons cannot re-enter the matrix, the gradient steepens, and pumping against that steep gradient becomes energetically prohibitive — so electron transport, and therefore O2 reduction at complex IV, slows to ~15% of baseline. This is respiratory control. DNP carries H+ back across the inner membrane, collapsing the gradient and removing the backpressure, so the chain runs even faster than at baseline (130%), burning succinate and reducing O2 with the free energy released as heat. ATP stays at zero because there is no gradient to drive synthesis and the synthase is inhibited anyway. B is wrong: DNP is a protonophore, not an electron carrier, and shunting electrons around the cytochromes would not raise O2 consumption at complex IV. C is wrong: DNP does not interact with ATP synthase's catalytic site, and reverse-running synthase would pump protons that DNP immediately dissipates. D is the most attractive distractor — it invokes respiratory control but inverts it: ADP was abundant at baseline and after oligomycin, yet O2 consumption fell, so ADP availability cannot explain the rise. Students who memorize "ADP stimulates respiration" without understanding that the gradient itself is the regulator pick D.

questions.subject: AP Macroeconomics
questions.question:
The economy of Meridia is producing below full employment. Its legislature enacts a large increase in government spending, financed entirely by selling new government bonds to the public. At the same time, Meridia's central bank announces that it will conduct open market operations as needed to keep the nominal interest rate unchanged at its current target. Assume flexible exchange rates and highly mobile international financial capital.

Which of the following best describes the short-run result of these combined policies?

choices.A: The central bank must buy bonds, increasing the money supply, and the crowding-out effect on private investment is eliminated.
choices.B: The central bank must sell bonds, decreasing the money supply, and the resulting increase in aggregate demand is smaller than it would be if the money supply were held constant.
choices.C: The money supply remains unchanged because the demand for money falls, which offsets any upward pressure on the nominal interest rate.
choices.D: Financial capital flows into Meridia and its currency appreciates, reducing net exports and partially offsetting the fiscal expansion.

questions.explanation:
The spending increase raises real output and income, which increases the transactions demand for money and puts upward pressure on the nominal interest rate. To hold the rate at its target, the central bank must accommodate by buying bonds, which increases the money supply and shifts money supply right by exactly enough to meet the higher money demand at the target rate. Because the interest rate never rises, private investment is not crowded out, and the full multiplier effect on AD is realized.

B reverses the required open market operation: selling bonds would push the rate up, not hold it constant, and it confuses accommodation with offsetting. C misidentifies the direction of the money-demand shift — rising income increases, not decreases, money demand. D describes the standard chain that occurs under a fixed money supply (rate rises, capital inflow, appreciation, net exports fall). Here the interest rate is pegged, so no interest-rate differential emerges and that chain is not triggered — this is the distractor that catches students who apply the memorized crowding-out/appreciation sequence without noticing the central bank's accommodating stance.

questions.subject: AP Statistics
questions.question:
A nutrition researcher wants to know whether a new label design increases the proportion of shoppers who buy a low-sodium soup. She recruits 400 volunteer shoppers at one supermarket. Because she suspects the effect differs by prior soup-buying habit, she first sorts the volunteers into "frequent soup buyers" (n = 160) and "infrequent soup buyers" (n = 240). Within each group, she randomly assigns half to see the new label and half to see the old label, then records purchases. Which statement best describes what this design permits?

A) Because the assignment is random within each group, results generalize to all shoppers at supermarkets nationwide.
B) A cause-and-effect conclusion about label design is justified for these volunteers, but generalization to a larger population is not.
C) Blocking on buying habit removes confounding by buying habit and therefore allows generalization to all shoppers.
D) No cause-and-effect conclusion is justified because the shoppers were volunteers rather than a random sample.

choices.A: Because the assignment is random within each group, results generalize to all shoppers at supermarkets nationwide.
choices.B: A cause-and-effect conclusion about label design is justified for these volunteers, but generalization to a larger population is not.
choices.C: Blocking on buying habit removes confounding by buying habit and therefore allows generalization to all shoppers.
choices.D: No cause-and-effect conclusion is justified because the shoppers were volunteers rather than a random sample.

questions.explanation:
This is a randomized block experiment: buying habit is the blocking variable, and treatments (new vs. old label) are randomly assigned within each block. Random ASSIGNMENT is what licenses causal inference, because it balances lurking variables across treatment groups on average. Random SELECTION from a population is what licenses generalization. Here there is random assignment but no random selection — the subjects are volunteers at a single supermarket — so causation is supported for this group while generalization is not. B captures exactly this split.

A confuses random assignment with random selection; random assignment within blocks does nothing to make a volunteer sample representative of shoppers nationwide.

C is a common trap: blocking does control for the blocking variable and improves precision by removing habit-related variability from the error, but blocking is a feature of the assignment scheme, not the sampling scheme, so it cannot create generalizability.

D reverses the two principles — it treats the absence of random selection as fatal to causal inference. Volunteers can still support a causal conclusion about themselves precisely because treatments were randomly assigned; the volunteer recruitment limits scope of inference, not the causal claim.

questions.subject: AP Computer Science A

choices.A: 9 is returned, and mystery is called 5 times.
choices.B: 9 is returned, and mystery is called 9 times.
choices.C: 7 is returned, and mystery is called 9 times.
choices.D: 9 is returned, and mystery is called 4 times.

questions.explanation: The method returns the maximum element via divide and conquer, so the returned value is 9. Counting calls: mystery(0,4) computes mid = 2 and calls mystery(0,2) and mystery(3,4). mystery(0,2) has mid = 1 and calls mystery(0,1) and mystery(2,2); mystery(0,1) has mid = 0 and calls mystery(0,0) and mystery(1,1). mystery(3,4) has mid = 3 and calls mystery(3,3) and mystery(4,4). That is 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 9 total calls. Note that lo > hi never occurs here, since each split with lo < hi produces two nonempty halves. Choice A reflects the common error of counting only the base-case calls (one per array element, 5). Choice D counts only the calls that recurse (the internal nodes of the call tree) and omits the base cases. Choice C returns 7 by mistakenly assuming the method returns the last element, or by treating the final comparison as returning right whenever left >= right on the top-level combine — but at the top level left = 9 (max of {4, 9, 2}) and right = 9 (max of {9, 7}), and since left > right is false the method returns right, which is 9, not 7.

questions.subject: AP English Language and Composition
questions.question:
The following is an excerpt from an 1871 address opposing the closing of a town's public reading room.

"I do not doubt the sincerity of the gentlemen who would close the reading room. They have seen what I have seen: the idle apprentice, the novel devoured at noon, the ledger left unbalanced. Their alarm is not manufactured; it is earned. But alarm is a poor architect. It builds walls where it meant to build a house, and then wonders that the family will not live in it. If the apprentice reads badly, the remedy is not fewer books but better ones, and a shelf near enough to reach without stealing. Lock the door, and you have not cured his appetite; you have only chosen who shall feed it."

The last sentence primarily functions to

(A) concede that the opponents' diagnosis of the apprentice's character was accurate
(B) recast the opponents' restriction as an act for which they bear responsibility
(C) evoke sympathy for the apprentice as the victim of forces beyond his control
(D) qualify the speaker's proposed remedy by admitting its limits

choices.A: concede that the opponents' diagnosis of the apprentice's character was accurate
choices.B: recast the opponents' restriction as an act for which they bear responsibility
choices.C: evoke sympathy for the apprentice as the victim of forces beyond his control
choices.D: qualify the speaker's proposed remedy by admitting its limits

questions.explanation:
The sentence turns on the verb "chosen." The opponents imagine closing the reading room as withdrawal — a neutral refusal to supply. The speaker denies them that neutrality: the appetite persists regardless, so the only thing their vote decides is which supplier ("who shall feed it") the apprentice turns to. Locking the door is thus not abstention but an active selection of a worse source, and the consequences are theirs to own. The imperative "Lock the door" plus the direct address "you have only chosen" fixes agency on the audience.

(A) misfires on scope. The speaker does concede — "Their alarm is not manufactured; it is earned" — but that concession is earlier, and it grants the accuracy of their *alarm*, not a diagnosis of character. The final sentence is the counterattack the concession set up, not more concession. Students who register "this is a conciliatory speaker" and generalize pick A.

(C) misreads the tone. "Appetite" is diagnostic, not pathetic; the apprentice is a case, not a sufferer. The passage's sympathy, such as it is, is aimed at the opponents ("I do not doubt the sincerity"). Nothing frames the apprentice as overpowered — indeed "without stealing" implies he acts.

(D) inverts the rhetorical direction. "You have not cured his appetite" describes what *their* policy fails to do, not what the speaker's does; it is an attack on the opposing remedy, not a hedge on his own. Students who see "not cured" and reflexively read qualification miss whose policy is the grammatical subject.

questions.subject: AP Chemistry
questions.question:
For the gas-phase reaction

    2 NO2(g) ⇌ N2O4(g)

ΔH° = -57.2 kJ/mol(rxn) and ΔS° = -175.8 J/(mol(rxn)·K), and both may be assumed independent of temperature.

A rigid, sealed flask containing an equilibrium mixture of NO2 and N2O4 at 298 K is heated to 400. K and allowed to re-establish equilibrium.

Which of the following best describes the equilibrium constant K for the reaction as written at 400. K, compared with 298 K?

(R = 8.314 J/(mol·K))

choices.A: K decreases to a value less than 1, and the equilibrium mixture at 400. K contains a greater proportion of NO2 than it did at 298 K.
choices.B: K decreases but remains greater than 1, because an exothermic reaction is thermodynamically favorable at every temperature.
choices.C: K increases, because raising the temperature increases the fraction of collisions with sufficient energy and therefore drives the reaction further toward products.
choices.D: K is essentially unchanged, because the flask is rigid, so neither the total volume nor the total number of gas molecules is altered by heating.

questions.explanation:
Use ΔG° = ΔH° - TΔS° and ΔG° = -RT ln K.

At 298 K: ΔG° = -57.2 kJ - (298 K)(-0.1758 kJ/K) = -57.2 + 52.4 = -4.8 kJ. Since ΔG° < 0, K > 1 at 298 K.

At 400. K: ΔG° = -57.2 kJ - (400. K)(-0.1758 kJ/K) = -57.2 + 70.3 = +13.1 kJ. Since ΔG° > 0, K < 1 (K = e^(-13100/(8.314×400)) ≈ 0.02).

Because both ΔH° and ΔS° are negative, the reaction is favorable only below the crossover temperature T = ΔH°/ΔS° = 57200/175.8 ≈ 325 K. Heating from 298 K to 400. K crosses that threshold, so K drops below 1 and the position of equilibrium shifts left (consistent with Le Châtelier: heat is a product of an exothermic reaction), leaving relatively more NO2.

Why the distractors fail:
B — Confuses a favorable enthalpy with a favorable ΔG°. With ΔS° < 0, the -TΔS° term is positive and grows with T; above ~325 K it overwhelms ΔH° and ΔG° becomes positive, so K falls below 1. Students who track only the sign of ΔH° stop at "K decreases" without checking the crossover.
C — The classic kinetics/thermodynamics conflation. Higher T does increase collision energy and speeds attainment of equilibrium, but K is fixed by ΔG°, not by rate; for an exothermic reaction K must decrease with T.
D — Constant volume does not fix K. K depends only on temperature; changing T changes ΔG° and therefore K, regardless of rigidity.
